+

Your first template

+

+ A template is just text with {t("{{ }}")} holes that data fills in. + Edit the template or the data below and watch it render — through the same engine + the FlatBars Lab ships. +

+ +

That's the whole loop: template + data → text. Now let's pick the right tool.

+
+ + +
+

Which dialect?

+

+ FlatBars isn't one language — it's a meaning-free core with four surfaces built on + it. They aren't tiers of quality; pick by your constraint, not by prestige. +

+ + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + +
Your jobUseWhy
Logic-less email / CMS snippets; Mustache parityMinBarsthe smallest surface — one sitting to learn it all; 184/184 of the Mustache spec
Importing existing Handlebars templatesFullBarsHandlebars-faithful (49/50 vs the real engine); your team already knows it
App views with real expressions (x > 3, pipes, loop vars)MaxBarsthe flagship surface — infix operators, pipes, bare loop variables
Building your own engine on the coreRawBarsthe austere, meaning-free substrate the others desugar to
+

+ It's a superset ladder — RawBars ⊂ FullBars ⊂ MaxBars — plus logic-less MinBars + off to the side. The MinBars reference is the recommended + place to learn the language; the rest of this page is the recommended + first ten minutes. +

+
+ + +
+

Keep templates dumb: shape data in the host

+

+ The single habit that keeps templates portable and reviewable: do the logic + where you have a real language, and hand the template a view-model it can walk + without branching. Here is the whole idea in one cell — a flat list of commits, a + transform that groups and labels them, and a template with zero branching: +

+ +

+ All the decisions live upstream, as data; the template just iterates. When the + reshaping gets real, that middle step is JSONata — and, + as the next section shows, it's also how you sidestep the one real trap. +

+
+ + +
+

The one trap: truthiness

+

+ false and null are falsy everywhere — portable. The other + four — 0, "", [], {t("{}")} — + are not, and engines disagree. In MinBars (and the language-agnostic + Mustache spec) 0 is truthy, so a section over count: 0 + renders: +

+ +

+ Hand the same count: 0 to Handlebars (FullBars), where + 0 is falsy, and the identical question takes the + opposite branch: +

+ +
+ Same data, opposite output — that's the trap. Don't memorize four falsy + tables. Two fixes, in order of preference: (1) shape the ambiguity out in the + host (the previous section) so the template never asks an ambiguous question; (2) + ask explicitly — {t("{{#if (ne count 0)}}")}. The + Truthiness analyser renders your template against your real + data and flags every condition that would flip — with a rule-free fix. +
+

+ One sharp edge: mustache.js (the JS implementation) treats + 0/"" as falsy like Handlebars, not like the spec; + and MaxBars uses a third rule again (nonEmpty: 0 truthy, + but ""/[]/{t("{}")} falsy). Which is the real + reason to lean on data prep, not on truthiness. +

+
+ + +
+

When {t("{{#if}}")} isn't enough → MaxBars

+

+ Start where your team is. In FullBars a condition is a Handlebars + subexpression — a helper application, {t("(gte score 90)")}: +

+
+
+
FullBars — subexpression
+ +
+
+
MaxBars — infix
+ +
+
+

+ The day {t("(gte score 90)")} wants to read score >= 90 + — with &&, pipes (value | helper), and bare loop + variables — that's MaxBars. It's the same engine and prelude + as FullBars, just an expression surface on top; you don't restart, you grow into it. +

+
+ + +
+
